keyVerseText: Speak unto the children of Israel, that they bring me an offering: of every man that giveth it willingly with his heart ye shall take my offering. bring me: Heb. take for me offering: or, heave offering
rootMeaning: The Hebrew verb נָדַב (nâdab) is a primitive root that conveys the core idea of willing or voluntarily offering oneself or something else. Its fundamental sense involves an inner impulse or incitement to act freely and generously, beyond mere obligation. This root meaning enriches the English glosses by emphasizing not only the act of giving but the motivated, spontaneous willingness behind it.
usageInScripture: Across its 17 occurrences, נָדַב consistently appears in contexts of voluntary giving or offering, often with the nuance of readiness and heartfelt willingness. The top translations such as "offered willingly," "made willing," and "that offered themselves willingly" reveal a spectrum from internal motivation to external action, highlighting both the incitement to give and the actual freewill offering. This consistency underscores the theme of voluntary devotion in the biblical narrative.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding נָדַב deepens our appreciation of biblical offerings as acts of the heart, not mere ritual compliance. It teaches that true worship involves a willing and generous spirit, reflecting God’s own gracious nature. This voluntary giving points forward to Christ, who offered Himself willingly for our redemption, setting the ultimate example of self-giving love. For believers, this word challenges us to examine the posture of our hearts in service and generosity toward God and others, emphasizing that God values the willing giver above all.
keyVerseReflection: Exodus 25:2 commands the Israelites to bring offerings only from those who "giveth it willingly with his heart." The use of נָדַב here highlights that God desires not just the gift but the willing and heartfelt disposition behind it. This verse teaches that offerings are accepted by God when they flow from genuine willingness, reinforcing the principle that worship is a matter of the heart, not compulsion.
